lines.text: A kingdom of green hills by Lake Tanganyika, ruled by kings, then by foreigners, then torn by violence before finding peace. This is Burundi.
In the seventeenth century a kingdom took shape in these hills, ruled by the mwami, the king.
In the 1880s Germany claimed a vast colony in East Africa, and Burundi was drawn into it.
In 1889 the Germans set up a post on Lake Tanganyika. It grew into Bujumbura, the largest city.
Inland, Gitega, the old royal seat, became a colonial town. Today it is the capital again.
After the First World War, Belgium took over, ruling Ruanda-Urundi for the League of Nations and later the UN.
Prince Louis Rwagasore led the push for independence. Weeks after his party won the 1961 election, he was murdered.
Melchior Ndadaye, born in 1953, would become the first elected Hutu president.
In 1962 Burundi became independent from Belgium, a small and crowded country in the hills of the Great Lakes.
Pierre Nkurunziza was born in 1964. He would go from rebel leader to president.
Evariste Ndayishimiye, born in 1968, would become president in 2020.
In 1972 came the Ikiza, the catastrophe, when the army killed many thousands of Hutu.
In 1993 Ndadaye was killed in a coup months after taking office, and a civil war began that lasted twelve years.
After decades of killing, Burundi's people still seek a lasting peace in their green hills.
